Asymptotic Variance of Stationary Availability

Source: R/04_savail.R
vcov_savail.Rd

Compute the asymptotic variance of the plug-in stationary availability estimator for an irreducible finite-state Markov chain.

Usage

vcov_savail(x, up)

Arguments

x

An object of class MarkovChain.

up

Integer-valued numeric vector of state positions or character vector of state names giving the operational states. Missing values are not allowed. Duplicates are ignored; empty and full state sets are valid. States are used in their order in x.

Value

A numeric scalar containing the variance in the \(\sqrt{n}\) limit of the stationary availability estimator. Divide by the number of observed transitions \(n\) to approximate the variance of the estimator itself.

Details

Equation (60) in Proposition 12 of Gavrilopoulos, Trevezas, and Votsi (2026) gives the limiting variable \(W_\pi e_U\). Consequently, $$\sigma^2_{A_\infty} = e_U^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_\pi e_U,$$ where \(\Sigma_\pi\) is the stationary-distribution asymptotic covariance from Proposition 7, computed by vcov_stat(). The function sums all entries of its operational-state submatrix, including the off-diagonal covariances. Since the stationary probabilities sum to one, the complementary state set has the same variance; the smaller set is used to reduce summation and cancellation. Empty and full sets return exactly zero after checking irreducibility.

The result does not depend on the initial distribution. This is the asymptotic variance of the transition-MLE plug-in estimator of stationary availability. The numerical conditioning limitations of vcov_stat() also apply here.

References

Gavrilopoulos, G., Trevezas, S., and Votsi, I. (2026). Matrix asymptotic calculus for plug-in maximum likelihood estimators in finite Markov chains. arXiv preprint arXiv:2607.17161. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17161.

See also

savail(), vcov_stat(), vcov_avail()

Examples

P <- matrix(c(0.8, 0.2, 0.3, 0.7), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
x <- MarkovChain(c(0.4, 0.6), P)
savail(x, up = 1L)
#> [1] 0.6
vcov_savail(x, up = 1L)
#> [1] 0.72
